author: Pooja Pawar, PhD
headline: Data Analyst | Business Intelligence & Data Visualization | 190K+ Data & Tech Community Across Platforms | Top 127 Global Data Science Creators (Favikon)
text:
SQL Interview Series – Day 13 #KPMG⁣⁣
⁣⁣

𝐓𝐚𝘀𝗸:⁣⁣
Write a SQL query to find the most recent order date for every customer in the orders table.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
This is a commonly asked question in SQL interviews at companies like 𝐊𝐏𝐌𝐆, 𝐙𝐒 𝐀𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 and 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝗼𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲, particularly for roles involving business analysis, reporting, and customer analytics. It evaluates your ability to apply aggregation functions and group-level logic in customer-focused data.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

𝐇𝗼𝘄 𝐭𝗼 𝐟𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝐢𝘁:⁣⁣
To solve this, group the records by customer_id, and use the MAX(order_date) function to identify the most recent order for each customer. This approach works well when you only need to retrieve the latest order date per customer and not the entire order details.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
This pattern is frequently used in loyalty programs, CRM updates, churn prediction, and behavioral segmentation.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

𝐂𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱:⁣⁣

1. 𝐆𝗥𝗢𝗨𝗣 𝗕𝘆 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲:⁣⁣
The dataset is grouped by each customer so that the aggregation function calculates one result per customer, rather than over the entire table.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
2. 𝐌𝐀𝗫() 𝐀𝗴𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:⁣⁣
The MAX() function retrieves the most recent (maximum) order date within each group of customer records. It’s efficient and supported across all major SQL platforms.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
3. 𝐀𝗹𝗶𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀:⁣⁣
The result of the MAX(order_date) is aliased as last_order, making the result more readable and suitable for further processing or export.⁣⁣
 ⁣⁣
4. 𝐒𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗲-𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗦𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗼𝘀:⁣⁣
This method is ideal when you’re only interested in knowing when a customer last placed an order, not what they ordered or how much they spent.⁣⁣
 ⁣⁣
5. 𝐄𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗥𝗢𝗪_𝗡𝗨𝗠𝗕𝗘𝗥():⁣⁣
If the interview question evolves to retrieving the entire latest order row per customer (including order ID, amount, or product), you can use ROW_NUMBER() with PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC in a CTE or subquery.⁣⁣
 ⁣⁣
6. 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲:⁣⁣
This logic is essential for scenarios like triggering re-engagement campaigns, identifying dormant customers, or updating dashboards with recent transaction summaries.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱:⁣⁣
Interviewers use this question to assess your understanding of grouping and aggregation functions. It’s also a gateway into more advanced topics such as window functions, filtering over partitions, and analytics-driven reporting. Candidates who provide both basic and extended answers (using ROW_NUMBER() when needed) demonstrate readiness for real-world data challenges.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

author: Bhavesh Arora
headline: Fintech | NTT Data | Talks about Fintech and Marketing, AI | 158k+ on Linkedin
text:
I cracked American Express in my first attempt! 🚀✌️
Here are 11 DSA + SQL problems I repeatedly practised before the interview:

𝟏. 𝐆𝐫𝗼𝘂𝗽 𝐀𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗺𝘀: Hashing, Strings
𝟐. 𝐓𝗼𝗽 𝐊 𝐅𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗘𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀: Heap, HashMap
𝟑. 𝐒𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗪𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗼𝘄 𝗠𝗮𝘅𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗺: Deque, Arrays
𝟒. 𝐌𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘀: Sorting, Greedy
𝟓. 𝐓𝘄𝗼 𝗦𝘂𝗺: Arrays, Hashing
𝟔. 𝐒𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗿𝘆: SQL, Window Functions
𝟳. 𝐂𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗡𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱: SQL Joins
𝟴. 𝐓𝗼𝗽 𝟯 𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗘𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝘁: SQL Window Functions
𝟵. 𝗠𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 / 𝗥𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝘂𝗺: SQL Frame Functions
𝟭𝟬. 𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿-𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿-𝗬𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵: SQL Self Joins
𝟭𝟭. 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝘆 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝗿𝘆: SQL CASE, COALESCE, Data Cleanup

Simply knowing SQL or DSA isn’t enough; you need to know how to extract insight, think in business terms, and communicate clearly.

It took me 4 months of case-solving and SQL breakdowns to figure this out. But you can skip all that trial and error by learning directly from Senior Data Scientists who’ve interviewed at your target companies. 💪
You can connect with them for FREE here: https://lnkd.in/dgGwHrVU

They’ll give you a personalized prep roadmap, insider tips for specific companies, and feedback on your approach, optimization, and communication — everything you need to crack your dream job. ✨

author: SWATI SINGH
headline: Associate Staff Engineer @Nagarro || Ex-TCS
text:
𝐏𝐞𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗻 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲 —
"You're still in TCS?"
But for me, it wasn’t “𝒔𝘵𝒊𝒍𝘭” — it was “𝐭𝐡𝗮𝗻𝗸𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹𝘆”.

𝐋𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲, 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵, 𝘇𝗲𝗿𝗼 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 — 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗹𝗼𝘀𝘁: 𝗵𝗼𝗽𝗲.
The past 2–3 years tested me in every possible way.
While the world was navigating through uncertainty, layoffs, and recession —
I was quietly fighting my own battle: recovering from a major surgery, and rebuilding myself physically, mentally, and emotionally.
There were days when friends and colleagues were getting promotions, flying abroad, and achieving milestones —
and I was just trying to stand again, one day at a time.

When I was at my lowest, 𝐓𝐂𝐒 𝐡𝗲𝗹𝗱 𝗺𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴.
✅ They gave me projects with full WFH flexibility.
✅ They gave me time to heal, grow, and rebuild myself without fear.
✅ They never made me feel like a burden, even when I was lying on my bed while others were hustling in offices.
In a time when 𝐣𝗼𝗯 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 felt like a myth, TCS gave me exactly that.
That kind of support? Rare.
And 𝐈’𝐥𝗹 𝗮𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗯𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗳𝘂𝗹.

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 — 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗻.
Growth often means stepping beyond what's familiar and safe.

So, with a heart full of gratitude,
𝐈’𝐦 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱 — 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗿𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜’𝘃𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝗧𝗖𝗦 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗲.
Thank you, TCS, for being my foundation during the most crucial phase of my life.
Here’s to embracing new challenges, dreaming bigger, and writing the next chapter with courage. 

𝙎𝙞𝙜𝙣𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙤𝗳𝗳 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 TCS (Tata Consultancy Services )— 𝙅𝘂𝗹𝘆 2021 𝘁𝗼 𝗝𝘂𝗹𝘆 2025. 🫶

Attaching some beautiful memories with the amazing friends and colleagues from my last client 𝗜𝗡𝗩𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗢, who made my return to office last year truly unforgettable. 💛📸
